props.title: Orphée

sections.content: Jean Cocteau's Orphée revolutionized mythological cinema by transplanting the Greek legend of Orpheus into post-war Paris. The film transforms Death into a mysterious princess traveling by Rolls-Royce, while poetry emanates from car radios in cryptic messages. This masterpiece influenced countless directors - you can see its DNA in Pan's Labyrinth (2006) and The Shape of Water (2017). Cocteau's practical effects, including his famous mercury mirror portals, created surreal magic without CGI that still captivates viewers today.

sections.content: The French New Wave directors worshipped Cocteau's ability to blend reality and fantasy. Last Year at Marienbad (1961) borrowed his mirror imagery and dreamlike atmosphere. Wings of Desire (1987) echoed Orphée's poetic vision of supernatural beings walking among mortals in a modern city. Even La La Land (2016) pays subtle homage to Cocteau's theatrical staging and romantic magical realism.

Orphée's influence extends deep into horror and dark fantasy. Suspiria (1977) directly references the film's mirror passages, while A Ghost Story (2017) echoes its meditation on death and eternal love. The way Cocteau shoots the underworld sequences - all reversed footage and practical effects - influenced The Wizard of Oz (1939) and continues to inspire filmmakers like Guillermo del Toro. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Practical Effects

sections.content: Modern fantasy films still reference Cocteau's innovative techniques. The Dark Knight (2008) used similar practical mirror effects for its interrogation scene, while Doctor Strange (2016) digitally reimagined Cocteau's reality-bending visuals. Inception (2010) director Christopher Nolan has cited Orphée as a major influence on his approach to practical effects over CGI.
